articles.title: Combined melatonin and edaravone therapy attenuates methylmercury-induced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like neurodegeneration through GLP-1 modulation and myelin preservation.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, resulting in progressive muscle weakness, paralysis, and respiratory failure. Despite the availability of disease-modifying therapies, current treatment options provide only modest clinical benefits, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting multiple pathological mechanisms. Melatonin, a pleiotropic neuroprotective molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, has emerged as a promising candidate; however, its influence on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-associated neuroprotective signaling and related molecular events in ALS remains poorly understood. Therefore, the present study investigated the neuroprotective efficacy of melatonin in a methylmercury (MTMR)-induced rat model of ALS and explored its effects on GLP-1-associated molecular alterations, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, demyelination, and neuronal injury. Molecular docking analysis was performed to predict the interaction of melatonin with proteins implicated in ALS pathology. Adult Wistar rats were exposed to MTMR (5 mg/kg, p.o.) for 21 days to induce ALS-like neurodegeneration, followed by treatment with melatonin (5 or 10 mg/kg, i.p.), edaravone (3 mg/kg, i.p.), or their combination for an additional 21 days. Neurobehavioral performance, biochemical alterations, hematological parameters, molecular biomarkers, and histopathological changes were subsequently evaluated. MTMR administration produced profound motor deficits accompanied by reduced GLP-1 levels, neurotransmitter imbalance, increased neuroinflammatory and apoptotic markers, elevated neurofilament light chain (NEFL), skeletal muscle injury, methylmercury accumulation, and extensive myelin and neuronal damage. Melatonin treatment significantly attenuated these pathological alterations in a dose-dependent manner by increasing GLP-1 levels, improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory and apoptotic responses, restoring neurotransmitter balance, preserving myelin integrity, and improving neuronal morphology across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord. Molecular docking further predicted favorable interactions between melatonin and several proteins associated with ALS pathophysiology, supporting its potential as a multitarget therapeutic agent. In most outcome measures, combined treatment with melatonin and edaravone produced greater neuroprotective effects than either intervention alone. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that melatonin substantially attenuates methylmercury-induced ALS-like neuropathology through coordinated modulation of multiple pathological processes associated with neurodegeneration. Although the precise molecular mechanisms require further experimental validation, the observed restoration of GLP-1 levels together with improvements in oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, neurotransmitter homeostasis, and myelin integrity suggests that melatonin may represent a promising adjunctive therapeutic strategy for ALS.

articles.title: Improving dysarthric speech classification with generative AI-based data augmentation.
articles.abstract: Dysarthria is a neurological speech disorder characterized by impaired motor control of speech production, resulting in reduced intelligibility. It commonly arises in the context of neurodegenerative conditions, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and cerebral palsy. The development of deep learning systems for dysarthria assessment is hindered by the scarcity of annotated data, which restricts the ability of models to generalize to unseen speakers. This study proposes a cross-corpus diffusion-based data augmentation strategy for improving automatic speech intelligibility classification from dysarthric speech. A Grad-TTS model is trained on dysarthric speakers from the TORGO dataset and used to synthesize the vocabulary of UA-Speech, producing speaker-conditioned samples intended to transfer pathological acoustic traits across corpora. The proposed strategy is evaluated both independently and in combination with conventional signal-level augmentation using ResNet-50 and ResNet-152 classifiers in binary and four-class intelligibility classification tasks. The results indicate that cross-corpus synthetic augmentation improves average performance and that, in most settings, its integration with conventional augmentation yields further gains, suggesting that the two strategies introduce complementary forms of variability.

articles.title: Longitudinal coagulation-fibrinolysis dynamics are associated with survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Background : Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has been associated with thromboembolic risk. However, whether dynamic coagulation-fibrinolysis markers provide prognostic information in ALS remains insufficiently defined. Methods : We conducted a prospective cohort study of 151 patients with ALS, including repeated coagulation measurements in a longitudinal subset ( n = 58), and assessed directional validation in the independent Answer ALS (AALS) cohort ( n = 270). Survival analyses, longitudinal modeling, and plasma proteomic analyses were used to examine associations between coagulation-fibrinolysis dynamics, functional decline, and survival. Results : Higher baseline fibrinogen (FIB) was independently associated with shorter survival (HR = 2.19; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.40-3.44). In the longitudinal subset, a steeper increase in D-dimer (DD) was associated with shorter survival (HR = 1.012; 95% CI, 1.001-1.024) and lower ALSFRS-R scores over time ( β = -0.013; 95% CI, -0.016 to -0.009). Directionally consistent validation was observed in AALS using rescaled SomaScan-derived DD trajectories (HR = 1.0002; 95% CI, 1.0000-1.0004). Plasma proteomics showed reduced tetranectin, a fibrinolysis-related protein, in ALS; slower tetranectin decline was associated with longer survival using rescaled SomaScan-derived tetranectin trajectories (HR = 0.996; 95% CI, 0.993-0.998). Conclusions : These findings suggest that longitudinal coagulation-fibrinolysis markers may help identify a survival-related biomarker profile in ALS, involving higher baseline FIB, steeper rising DD, and reduced or more rapidly declining tetranectin.

articles.title: Riluzole-Derived Benzo[d]thiazoles as CK1δ Inhibitors for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis-Related Neurodegeneration.
articles.abstract: Riluzole-derived benzo[d]thiazoles were investigated as metabolite-inspired CK1δ inhibitors, a kinase involved in TDP-43 phosphorylation and therefore relevant to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Starting from the known CK1δ activity of riluzole, we examined whether its major hydroxylamine metabolite could preserve target recognition and provide a rational entry point for scaffold optimisation. The metabolite retained CK1δ inhibition, but its limited chemical stability and toxicity in neuronal cells identified the hydroxylamine group as a critical liability. Replacement of this functionality with a hydrazine converted the fragile metabolite-derived structure into a more potent and tractable CK1δ inhibitor series. Structure-activity relationship studies revealed that the hydrazine moiety accommodates broader substitution than the hydroxylamine counterparts, with branched alkyl and benzyl groups giving the most balanced profiles. Docking and molecular dynamics suggested that the improvement could be attributed to an additional hydrogen-bond with Gly86 in the hinge region. The best derivative combined submicromolar CK1δ inhibition with passive blood-brain barrier permeability, short-term cellular tolerance, ATP competitive inhibition, direct target engagement, and preliminary selectivity over GSK3β. Although this compound did not result neuroprotective in an oxidative stress model, it paves the way for a focused benzo[d]thiazole platform for probing CK1δ biology in ALS.

articles.title: The Epidemiological Transition of Neurodegenerative Diseases in China: A Multi-Layered Deconstruction Using Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), including Alzheimer's disease and other dementias (ADOD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and motor neuron disease (MND), represent a mounting public health challenge in China amid rapid population aging. A systematic deconstruction of their epidemiological transition using the most recent data remains lacking. Data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 were utilized to examine temporal trends (1990-2023) for ADOD, PD, and MND in China. Age-standardized rates of incidence (ASIR), prevalence (ASPR), mortality (ASMR), and disability-adjusted life-years (ASDR) were analyzed. Joinpoint regression was used to identify significant inflection points. Decomposition analysis quantified the contributions of population aging, population growth, and epidemiological change. And bayesian age-period-cohort models projected trends to 2035. From 1990 to 2023, the ASIR for ADOD (EAPC 0.41; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.49) and PD (EAPC 0.84; 95% CI 0.76 to 0.92) rose significantly. Between 2019 and 2023, multiple indicators across the three diseases demonstrated a consistently synchronous upward trend. This acceleration coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic. Decomposition demonstrated that population aging was the dominant driver. Sex-specific disparities were pronounced. Females bore a higher ADOD burden, whereas males predominated in PD. ASIR and ASPR are expected to rise, while ASMR and ASDR are projected to decline for ADOD and PD. For MND, only the ASPR indicated a brief, peaked rise in the predicted trends. In the field of neurodegenerative diseases, China is projected to undergo an epidemiological transition characterized by chronicization. This trend calls for systematic adjustments in healthcare services, long-term care systems, and social support structures. Sex and gender differences further underscore the need for gender-sensitive prevention, clinical management, and care strategies to prevent the further widening of inequalities. Population aging remains a critical factor that cannot be overlooked. Therefore, there is an urgent need to establish a proactive, gender-sensitive framework for system-wide restructuring that incorporates long-term monitoring and oversight.

articles.title: Global best practice recommendations for genetic counselling and testing in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with substantial clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Advances in ALS genomics, emerging gene-targeted therapies, and genotype-specific clinical trials have increased the importance of genetic counselling and testing for individuals with ALS and their families. However, access to these services remains highly variable globally due to disparities in healthcare infrastructure, laboratory capacity, specialist availability, and funding. Existing guidance has largely been developed in high-resource settings and may not be feasible or equitable worldwide. The International Alliance of ALS/MND Associations convened an international, multidisciplinary Genetics Task Force to develop expert consensus recommendations for genetic counselling, genetic testing, and laboratory practice in ALS across diverse geographic and resource settings. Recommendations were developed through a structured, iterative consensus process incorporating clinical expertise, lived experience perspectives, published evidence, and global representation. Final recommendations were reviewed and approved through anonymous voting at an in-person consensus meeting. The resulting recommendations establish both minimum and aspirational best practices, emphasizing equitable access, informed decision-making, culturally responsive counselling, tiered genetic testing approaches, and context-appropriate laboratory standards. These globally informed recommendations provide a pragmatic framework to support clinicians, laboratories, policymakers, and advocacy organizations in improving access to high-quality ALS genetics services worldwide.
authors: Alliance Genetics Task Force Working Group Members

articles.title: Intracisternal injection of two human SOD1 aggregate strains induces templated aggregation and ALS in transgenic mouse model.
articles.abstract: Cytosolic aggregates containing misfolded superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) protein is an established hallmark of ALS caused by mutations in the SOD1 gene. We have previously identified two structurally distinct strains of human (h) SOD1 aggregates (denoted A and B) in mice transgenic (Tg) for hSOD1. Strain A and B have both been shown to transmit templated aggregation and induce early-onset of fatal ALS-like disease when injected directly into the spinal cord or peripheral nerve of hSOD1 Tg mice. In contrast, peripheral administration of hSOD1 aggregates into the intraperitoneal cavity or skeletal muscle did not induce disease. Collectively, these studies provide insight on the spreading mechanism of SOD1. However, the complete map of propagation routes and underlying mechanisms utilized by SOD1 aggregates in ALS is not fully charted. Here, we investigated whether hSOD1 aggregates may spread to the central nervous system (CNS) via the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Mutant hSOD1 aggregate seeds or control samples prepared from spinal cords of hSOD1 Tg mice or non-Tg mice, respectively, were inoculated into the cisterna magna of adult 100-day-old Tg mice expressing the G85R mutated hSOD1 protein. Disease phenotyping as well as biochemical and immunohistochemical analyses were performed and compared across the experimental groups. The mice inoculated with hSOD1 seeds developed early signs of ALS by 90 days after inoculation and reached terminal stage approximately 180 days earlier than mice receiving control seeds. Additionally, both strain A and B were observed to initiate templated aggregation along the neuroaxis. The results show that hSOD1 aggregates are capable of transmitting from the CSF to the CNS where they induce ALS-like pathology and concomitant phenotype. Unraveling the propagation pathways utilized by SOD1 opens new avenues to assess treatment strategies against ALS.

articles.title: Neuromuscular junction pathology in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and emerging molecular therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Traditionally conceptualized as a soma-centric pathology, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal, heterogeneous neurodegenerative disease. The suboptimal outcomes of central nervous system (CNS)-directed therapeutic strategies have necessitated a shift in focus toward the dying-back hypothesis. This hypothesis contends that synaptic disconnection and axonal retraction at the distal neuromuscular junction (NMJ) are early pathological events that may antedate overt motor neuron loss. This review systematically examines the NMJ as an early vulnerable and therapeutically tractable peripheral niche in ALS pathogenesis, rather than merely a downstream consequence of proximal proteinopathy. Evidence from human clinical samples and ALS mouse models, particularly SOD1-G93A mice, collectively supports the early vulnerability of the NMJ, with the temporal precedence of denervation, synaptic retraction, and mitochondrial dysfunction most clearly demonstrated in experimental models. We highlight how the breakdown of the tripartite synapse-comprising the motor terminal, skeletal muscle, and terminal Schwann cells (tSCs)-may disrupt essential neurotrophic signaling and local metabolic homeostasis. Furthermore, we discuss how advancements in humanized in vitro NMJ models and spatial transcriptomics provide unprecedented resolution into localized RNA dysmetabolism and bioenergetic failure. Finally, we evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies specifically designed to stabilize or restore the NMJ, including MuSK agonists and other NMJ-directed approaches. By recontextualizing the NMJ as a critical early site of vulnerability, we propose that targeting the peripheral synaptic microenvironment may offer a promising strategy for modifying the progression of ALS.

articles.title: Persistent and compartmentalized T cell immunity in ALS.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal neurodegenerative disease increasingly linked to T cell responses, although the mechanisms driving T cell activation and disease progression remain unclear. Here we used single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing, longitudinal immune profiling and imaging flow cytometry to identify long-lived intrathecal clonotypes and antigen-presenting cell-T cell complexes displaying features of immunological synapse formation, consistent with intrathecal antigen presentation. Higher frequencies of CD4 + effector, CD4 + regulatory and CD8 + T cells in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were associated with slower disease progression, whereas increased circulating CD4 + effector and regulatory T cells were associated with faster progression. T cell clonotypes shared between blood and CSF exhibited distinct transcriptional states. Finally, frequencies of cytomegalovirus-specific T cells in CSF and anticytomegalovirus serum antibodies were correlated with faster progression and shorter survival in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These findings reveal compartmentalized immune dynamics, largely contrasting protective intrathecal responses with harmful systemic activation.

articles.title: Rate and Shape of Functional Decline in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Identify Clinically Distinct Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Phenotypes.
articles.abstract: The ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised decline rate compresses trajectory shape into a single number, potentially missing distinct phenotypes. We tested whether shape identifies phenotypes that rate does not distinguish, and whether post-hoc analysis recovers a hidden ultrarapid subgroup. From the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta register (2000-2022), we applied 2 models to 1,686 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients: a Gaussian mixture model (GMM; rate axis) and a latent-class mixed model (LCMM) with cubic splines (shape axis). Concordance, prognostic performance, calibration, and clinical utility were assessed at 24 months. External validation used the Emilia-Romagna register. The rate model identified 4 classes (GMM-Slow 31%, GMM-Inter-slow 46%, GMM-Inter-fast 17%, GMM-Catastrophic 6%; slopes -0.44 to -3.52 points/month); the shape model 4 (LCMM-SlowLinear 46%, LCMM-PlateauFall 23%, LCMM-LateDecline 15%, LCMM-RapidEarly 16%). Concordance was modest (kappa = 0.273). Adding shape to rate changed discrimination negligibly (C-index 0.761 vs 0.755), but separated subgroups within rate classes (within GMM-Catastrophic, 30.1 vs 12.0 months). LCMM-LateDecline combined moderate early decline with reduced respiratory reserve (median forced vital capacity 83.5%) and 22.7-month median survival. The combined model gave the greatest net benefit for the composite outcome. Of 945 patients excluded for sparse sampling, 367 were ultrarapid progressors with shorter survival than LCMM-RapidEarly; findings replicated in the Emilia-Romagna register. Rate and shape describe partially overlapping aspects of the disease. LCMM-LateDecline, with moderate early decline yet occult respiratory compromise, is clinically challenging, and the 3-visit criterion hides over half of ultrarapid patients. Rate predicts the overall burden of progression, whereas shape predicts the timing of deterioration. ANN NEUROL 2026.

articles.title: Structural Social Connection, Biological Ageing, and Neurodegenerative Disease Burden: A Global Ecological Analysis of Household Size and Modelled Dementia Incidence Estimates.
articles.abstract: Poor social connection and ageing-related biological processes are recognised contributors to Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. However, cross-national evidence linking structural indicators of social connection with dementia and broader neurological dis-ease burden remains limited. This ecological study examined country-level associations be-tween average household size and modelled neurological disease incidence estimates. Country- and territory-level data from up to 204 settings were analysed. Average household size was the primary exposure, and model-derived, age-standardised incidence-rate estimates for Alzheimer's disease and other dementias were the primary outcome. Par-kinson's disease, motor neuron disease, multiple sclerosis, idiopathic epilepsy, headache dis-orders, and total neurological disorders were examined as comparative secondary outcomes. The Henneberg Index, life expectancy at age 60, GDP per capita, and urban living were in-cluded as contextual covariates. Analyses included Pearson and Spearman correlations, par-tial correlations, principal component analysis, and multivariable linear regression. Household size was strongly and inversely associated with Alzheimer's disease and other dementias incidence estimates (Pearson r=-.841, p<.001). The association remained after adjustment for the included covariates (β=-.569, p<.001). Significant inverse adjusted associations were also observed for Parkinson's disease, motor neuron disease, and total neurological disorders, whereas patterns differed for other neurological outcomes. Principal component analysis identified a single ageing-development dimension explaining 72.1% of the variance, with household size loading inversely against life expectancy at age 60, econom-ic affluence, urban living, and the Henneberg Index. Smaller average household size was associated with higher modelled incidence estimates for dementia and selected neurodegenerative diseases at the country level. These findings should be interpreted as ecological associations rather than evidence of individual-level causation and suggest that household structure is embedded within broader demograph-ic, socioeconomic, and ageing-related processes.

articles.title: TDP-43 dysfunction destabilizes glial homeostatic identity in ALS/FTD.
articles.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) pathology is a defining feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). Although TDP-43 dysfunction has traditionally been studied through a neuron-centric framework, increasing evidence demonstrates that astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes are also directly affected and actively contribute to disease progression. In this review, we examine how TDP-43 dysfunction disrupts lineage-specific glial homeostatic programs and promotes distinct pathological state transitions across major glial populations. In astrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction impairs neurotransmitter regulation, metabolic and neuronal support, RNA homeostasis, and secretory signaling while promoting inflammatory and antiviral-like states. In microglia, altered TDP-43 disrupts inflammatory regulation, phagocytosis, lysosomal function, lipid metabolism, and stage-dependent protective responses. In oligodendrocytes, TDP-43 dysfunction compromises RNA processing, lineage maintenance, lipid metabolism, myelin integrity, and long-term axonal support. Together, these findings suggest that glial TDP-43 dysfunction cannot be reduced to a single generalized form of reactivity but instead reflects the breakdown of distinct cell type-specific identities required to maintain central nervous system homeostasis. A cross-glial framework integrating cell-autonomous dysfunction, non-cell-autonomous signaling, disease stage, and genetic context may therefore provide a more complete understanding of TDP-43 proteinopathy and its contribution to neurodegeneration across the ALS-FTD spectrum.

articles.title: Time-to-Event Analysis of Clinical Milestones in the ALS Natural History Consortium Dataset.
articles.abstract: Study of clinical milestones, particularly intermediate events like loss of ambulation, in large amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cohorts is limited. Here, we leverage the ALS Natural History Consortium dataset to evaluate the time-to-event for several outcomes and prognostic factors that predict risk. Longitudinal data from 1950 participants were used in time-to-event analyses based on time from diagnosis. Outcomes were gastrostomy, loss of ambulation, loss of useful speech, non-invasive ventilation (NIV) usage, and death equivalent (death or mechanical ventilation). Median times-to-event were calculated along with Kaplan-Meier curves. Cox proportional hazards models for each outcome estimated (through adjusted hazard ratios [HR]) the impact of several prognostic factors, including sex, region of onset, age at diagnosis, and the initial rate of change (delta-FRS) in ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) scores. Estimated median times-to-event for clinical outcomes ranged from 1.44 to 6.21 years, with a median time to death equivalent of 2.12 years. A higher delta-FRS was the greatest risk factor for all outcomes (HRs between 2.01 and 3.05). Limb onset decreased risk of loss of speech, NIV use, gastrostomy, and death equivalent (HRs 0.41-0.78). Older age at diagnosis increased risk of gastrostomy, NIV use, and death equivalent (HRs 1.08-1.27). These findings further inform expectations of time to various outcomes, especially rarely investigated intermediate events, and their risk factors. The importance of progression rate supports other recent findings, highlighting delta-FRS as a key prognostic factor with potential utility in clinical trial designs.

articles.title: Diaphragm reserve utilisation in motor neurone disease: A novel ultrasound-derived physiological index.
articles.abstract: Respiratory involvement is a major determinant of prognosis in motor neurone disease (MND; or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), yet conventional static respiratory measures provide limited information about how much available diaphragm thickening capacity is recruited during quiet breathing. We evaluated diaphragm reserve utilisation (RU), an ultrasound-derived ratio of tidal diaphragm thickening relative to maximal diaphragm thickening, as a novel physiological descriptor in MND. In a prospective observational study, 38 patients with MND and 20 healthy controls underwent right hemidiaphragm ultrasound to measure thickness at end-tidal expiration, peak tidal inspiration and peak maximal inspiration. Thickening fractions and RU were calculated. Between-group differences in diaphragm ultrasound indices were assessed. Secondary analyses examined relationships between RU, respiratory function and survival. Tidal diaphragm thickening fraction was similar between patients with MND and controls, whereas maximal thickening fraction was lower in MND, resulting in higher RU in MND than controls. This pattern indicates that patients with MND maintained tidal diaphragm thickening while using a greater proportion of their available maximal thickening capacity. Higher RU was also associated with shorter survival, supporting its potential physiological and clinical relevance. Diaphragm reserve utilisation describes the proportion of measured diaphragm thickening capacity recruited during tidal breathing. Patients with MND demonstrated preserved tidal thickening despite reduced maximal thickening capacity, resulting in higher RU than healthy controls. This supports RU as a novel physiological index of relative diaphragm thickening reserve utilisation. The relationship between RU and survival warrants validation in larger prospective cohorts.

articles.title: Motor neuron disease and parkinsonism in a patient with a pathogenic CSF1R variant.
Respiratory Phenotypes for Stratifying and Predicting Survival in ALS.
articles.abstract: Phenotypic heterogeneity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an obstacle to stratification and survival prediction and is not sufficiently accounted for in clinical practice or trial design. We aimed to identify respiratory phenotypes to allow stratification and survival prediction in ALS. We retrospectively analyzed 292 ALS patients. Data included demographics, disease-related characteristics, and respiratory measurements (initial predicted forced vital capacity [FVC] and 3-month decline slope). Survival analysis was performed using Kaplan-Meier estimates and Cox regression. We defined four respiratory phenotypes based on dichotomized predicted FVC at the initial visit and its 3-month decline slope: (1) initial high, slow decline (IHSD), (2) initial high, fast decline (IHFD), (3) initial low, slow decline (ILSD), and (4) initial low, fast decline (ILFD). Patients with an initial predicted FVC above the median had a median survival of 33 months, compared to 15 months for those below the median (p < 0.0001). The highest quartile had an almost threefold survival advantage over the lowest quartile (37 vs. 13 months, p < 0.0001). A 3-month slope at or above the median predicted longer survival (33 vs. 14 months, p < 0.0001). Survival varied across respiratory phenotypes, ranging from 41 months in IHSD to 11 months in ILFD-with all comparisons being significant (p ≤ 0.0012) except for ILSD vs. IHFD. Defining respiratory phenotypes in ALS may allow tailored research within those subgroups, biomarker correlations, more accurate prognostication, and stratification in clinical trials based on phenotype-specific disease progression.

articles.title: ALS-associated cytoskeletal and glial gene expression: evidence consistent with developmental pathway re-engagement.
articles.abstract: We examined whether amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is associated with cytoskeletal and glial transcriptional patterns compatible with developmental pathway re-engagement, while recognizing that similar patterns may arise from injury responses and altered cell composition. Postmortem RNA-sequencing data from the Target ALS Postmortem Tissue Core were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models accounting for repeated tissue samples within subjects. Models were adjusted for tissue source, age at death, sex, and postmortem interval. Composite scores represented Arp2/3 activity, SOX9/MEGF10 developmental-glial expression, and MYH10-associated transport imbalance. ALS was associated with increased Arp2/3 expression (β = 0.399, P = 8.26 × 10 -9 ), SOX9/MEGF10 expression (β = 0.643, P = 4.28 × 10 -6 ), MYH10 expression (β = 0.308, P = 0.000801), and MYH10-KIF5C transport mismatch (β = 0.121, P = 0.00537); all remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction. The MYH10-Arp2/3 contractility index was not significant (β = -0.0909, P = 0.107). ALS was associated with higher expression of selected cytoskeletal and glial genes in bulk postmortem tissue. These cross-sectional associations are compatible with, but do not demonstrate, developmental program reactivation, altered protein activity, or causation. Cell-resolved and functional studies are needed.

articles.title: Cost-effectiveness of multidisciplinary care compared with standard neurology care in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A model-based cost-utility analysis.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of multidisciplinary clinic (MDC) care compared with standard general neurology care for adults with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). A cost-utility analysis was conducted using a state-transition Markov model with monthly cycles over a 10-year horizon from the U.S. payer perspective. Health states comprised King's stages 1, 2, 3, 4 A, 4B, and death. Disease progression, mortality, utility, and cost inputs were derived from published literature (2005-2026). Transition probabilities were based on longitudinal data from the Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials and permitted non-sequential progression. MDC-associated survival benefit was applied to stage-specific mortality across all King's stages. No additional utility benefit was assigned to MDC, while MDC-specific multipliers were applied to outpatient, inpatient, and emergency department costs. Outcomes included quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), costs, cost per life-year gained, and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). Uncertainty intervals (UIs) were derived from sensitivity analyses. MDC increased costs ($523,170 vs $378,171) and QALYs (0.73 vs 0.60), yielding 0.13 incremental QALYs (95% UI, 0.06-0.20) at an incremental cost of US$144,999 (95% UI, $53,784-$257,504). The ICER was US$1,158,673/QALY and cost per life-year gained was US$149,483. MDC was cost-effective in 0.1% of simulations at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $150,000/QALY. MDC improved survival and quality-adjusted survival but at substantially higher cost. Its ICER remained well above commonly used U.S. willingness-to-pay thresholds across sensitivity analyses, including alternative utility valuations. These findings highlight the distinction between clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness and quantify the long-term economic consequences of survival gains associated with multidisciplinary ALS care.

articles.title: Mild cognitive impairment in presymptomatic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are clinically and biologically related, and each may be preceded by a prodromal stage of disease. Mild cognitive and behavioural impairment (MCI/MBI) have also been observed in those with clinically manifest ALS. The primary aim of this study was to characterise MCI in presymptomatic ALS. Criteria for frontotemporal-related MCI (MCI-ft), which require evidence of subthreshold cognitive performance or decline, were adapted from existing frameworks for MCI in prodromal FTD, presymptomatic ALS and clinically manifest ALS. MCI-ft was characterised in 216 Pre-fALS participants (74 C9ORF72, 94 SOD1, 20 other pathogenic variant carriers and 28 non-carriers) with neuropsychological data at 807 study visits. All designations were reviewed by a research neuropsychologist, with consensus discussions as needed. MCI-ft was observed in 15 (20%) C9ORF72, 12 (13%) SOD1 and 3 (%) of other carriers at one or more study visits, compared to 1 (4%) non-carrier. Most visits with MCI-ft showed impairment affecting both language and executive functioning. Fluctuations in MCI-ft status between assessments were common. The observed frequency and temporal course of MCI-ft in presymptomatic ALS, using criteria based on subthreshold cognitive performance and decline, expands understanding of this phase of disease. These findings help to inform future research examining the risk of phenoconversion to clinically manifest disease and aid the design of disease prevention trials.

articles.title: Constructing functional neural circuits to model amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons. Recent advances in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids offer an innovative platform to model amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a human-specific context. These three-dimensional organoid systems allow for the study of neuronal circuit-level dysfunction, which is central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis pathogenesis, by incorporating multiple neuronal subtypes and supporting glial populations. In particular, the integration of region-specific brain organoids into assembloid models has enabled the reconstruction of functional long-range projections and cortico-motor circuits, closely resembling human neural connectivity. This review summarizes the generation and application of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research, with a focus on the reconstruction of neural circuits, multi-omics profiling, and functional assays. We also discuss how organoid systems can be leveraged for drug discovery and personalized medicine in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, highlighting their potential to unveil human-specific disease mechanisms. Lastly, we address the current challenges and future directions for improving the physiological relevance of organoid models in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research.

articles.title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
articles.abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

articles.title: Unlocking therapeutic potential of Wnt signaling pathway in neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.abstract: The Wnt Signaling pathway is a regulatory network that is highly conserved in the central nervous system and is essential for the survival of neurons, synaptic plasticity, and the blood-brain barrier's integrity. The pathophysiology of major neurodegenerative and neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and traumatic brain injury (TBI), is highly influenced by canonical and non-canonical Wnt Signaling dysregulation, according to increasingly compelling evidence. In addition to emphasising common molecular events such as GSK-3β overactivation, β-catenin destabilisation, neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and BBB disruption, this study offers a comparative and mechanistic overview of Wnt pathway changes across various illnesses. This article identifies overlapping treatment targets, such as GSK-3β, DKK1, LRP5/6, and Wnt ligands, by integrating common and disease-specific Wnt-associated pathways, in contrast to traditional disease-specific reviews. Furthermore, new translational approaches involving natural substances, Wnt modulators, and pathway-targeted treatments are critically examined. All things considered, this study presents Wnt Signaling as a potential neuroprotective and regenerative target for upcoming precision-based treatments in neurodegenerative disorders.

articles.title: Cellular senescence in ageing and neurodegenerative disorders: Molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Cellular senescence has been increasingly associated with neurodegenerative disorders, potentially linking ageing-related cellular impairment with mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and disrupted intercellular signalling. The present study aims to explore the increasing relevance of cellular senescence among key cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, neural progenitor cells, microglia and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells across neurodegenerative ailments such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis. This review discusses the findings of pre-clinical and clinical studies which suggest that senescence-associated features may contribute to neurodegeneration. Further, it provides an overview of the biomarkers used in the identification of senescence in the CNS. Also, the review examines senotherapeutic treatment approaches, highlighting their actions on different CNS cell types and the growing clinical evidence. It also points out the challenges in translating these approaches to clinical application, such as targeting specific cell types and the lack of suitable biomarkers. Collectively, present findings suggest that senescence-associated alterations may contribute to neurodegeneration, although their effects appear to vary across cell types and diseases.

articles.title: Drosophila Models of Human Neurodegenerative Diseases.
articles.abstract: In his book Insects and the Life of Man: Collected Essays on Pure Science and Applied Biology, Sir V. B. Wigglesworth examined how a fundamental understanding of insect physiology and biology can be applied to some of society's greatest challenges, including human health. Here we reflect on how, in the 50 years since his book's publication, Drosophila melanogaster have played a critical role in advancing our understanding of human neurodegenerative diseases. Focusing on Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and the frontotemporal dementia / amyotrophic lateral sclerosis spectrum, we examine the role Drosophila have played in elucidating fundamental mechanisms of neurodegeneration, identifying therapeutic targets, and dissecting the complex interplay that exists between genetics and environmental factors. Together these studies highlight how Drosophila models continue to provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms underpinning neurodegeneration and provide a fundamental pre-clinical model in which we can accelerate research into human neurodegenerative conditions.

articles.title: Feasibility and apparent safety of functional electrical stimulation-assisted cycling in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and primary lateral sclerosis: a single-arm longitudinal pilot feasibility study.
articles.abstract: Functional electrical stimulation-assisted cycling may be relevant in motor neuron disease, but its feasibility and safety in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and primary lateral sclerosis remain unclear. The authors aimed to assess feasibility, apparent safety, and exploratory pre-post clinical changes of a three-week functional electrical stimulation-assisted cycling protocol in ambulatory inpatients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or primary lateral sclerosis. Fifteen patients were assessed; 11 were enrolled (5 ALS, 6 PLS) and received 15 supervised 30-minute FES-cycling sessions over three weeks in addition to conventional neuromotor rehabilitation. Bilateral eight-channel stimulation targeted quadriceps, tibialis anterior, hamstrings, and gastrocnemius during active or active-assisted cycling. Feasibility outcomes were enrollment, completion, tolerance, adverse events, and pre-post data availability. Clinical outcomes were analyzed descriptively. Eleven of 15 assessed patients were enrolled (73.3%; 5 ALS, 6 PLS). All enrolled participants completed the protocol, no adverse events were documented, and complete pre-post data were available. Exploratory outcomes showed favorable short-term changes in mobility, walking, strength, and spasticity. This protocol appears feasible and apparently safe in selected ambulatory inpatients. Findings are hypothesis-generating and support a prospective controlled feasibility trial before efficacy is tested.

articles.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in neurology: biomarkers and clinical implications.
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared downstream pathogenic mechanism across a wide spectrum of neurological disorders, ranging from primary mitochondrial diseases to conditions including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, hereditary ataxias and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. This Review examines the role of mitochondrial biomarkers in improving diagnostic accuracy, patient stratification and monitoring of disease progression and therapeutic response. Primary mitochondrial diseases are presented as proof-of-concept models of impaired oxidative phosphorylation, providing a framework for biomarker identification and validation with translational relevance to other neurological diseases. Mitochondrial biomarkers can be broadly categorized into four domains: fluid biomarkers, reflecting metabolic alterations and stress signalling; genetic biomarkers, capturing mitochondrial DNA integrity and dynamics; multi-omics approaches, integrating transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic signatures; and imaging biomarkers, enabling in vivo assessment of structural and functional consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction. Across disorders, these biomarkers reveal shared disturbances in bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, mitochondrial genome maintenance and inflammatory signalling. However, clinical implementation remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, biological variability and reduced disease specificity. Integrated, multimodal biomarker strategies, combined with longitudinal validation, will be essential for supporting precision medicine and guiding the development of therapies to target mitochondrial pathways in neurology.

articles.title: Neurodegeneration in sub-Saharan Africa: Intersections of biological ageing, genomic diversity and the lifetime exposome.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are emerging as an important consequence of population ageing in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), but their scientific relevance extends beyond a projected rise in case numbers. SSA combines exceptional human genomic diversity with marked heterogeneity in vascular and metabolic risk, infection, nutrition, occupational exposures, air pollution, and access to health care. This combination creates an underused setting in which to study why biological ageing produces neurodegeneration in some individuals but relative resilience in others. This review critically synthesises evidence on Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/frontotemporal degeneration, Huntington's disease and related disorders, focusing on the intersection between hallmarks of ageing, disease-specific proteinopathies, ancestry and the lifetime exposome. Age-associated loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, chronic inflammation, neurovascular injury and genomic/epigenomic instability provide a mechanistic scaffold on which genetic susceptibility and cumulative exposures may act. Yet African evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional clinical phenotyping; neuropathology, longitudinal biomarkers, multi-omics and measured environmental exposures remain sparse. Recent African-ancestry Parkinson's disease genomics and emerging plasma biomarker studies demonstrate that ancestry-inclusive molecular neuroscience is feasible and can generate findings not predictable from European-ancestry datasets. The next phase should therefore move beyond documenting underdiagnosis toward longitudinal, biologically anchored cohorts that integrate phenotype, genomics, blood biomarkers, neuroimaging, exposomics, digital measures and health-system outcomes. This review proposes a research framework centred on biological ageing, gene-environment interaction and resilience. Such work would improve the validity of prevention, diagnosis and therapeutic translation in African populations while contributing globally to a more complete biology of neurodegenerative ageing.

articles.title: Neurodegenerative Diseases: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Classification, Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Strategies.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing cause of disability worldwide, particularly as populations age. Although these disorders differ in etiology and clinical presentation, advances in genetics, neuropathology, and biomarker research have identified shared disturbances in protein homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and immune regulation. These processes may contribute to selective neuronal vulnerability and neural circuit dysfunction. These findings are refining disease classification and diagnosis, yet effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Disease-specific abnormalities remain essential to clinical interpretation and treatment selection. Existing reviews often focus on individual disorders or isolated mechanisms, leaving the links between shared biology and disease-specific phenotypes insufficiently clear. We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, classification, and pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Friedreich's ataxia, and multiple sclerosis. We compare their clinical manifestations and diagnostic approaches, including the evolving role of biomarkers, and critically assess established and emerging therapies. By distinguishing shared mechanisms from disease-specific abnormalities, we identify key translational gaps and explore how common biological disturbances may lead to distinct clinical trajectories. This cross-disease perspective may inform diagnostic reasoning, treatment development, and future comparative research.

articles.title: State transitions in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: mechanistic convergence and biomarker-guided stratification.
articles.abstract: Biological heterogeneity is a major obstacle to therapeutic development in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Cross-sectional pathway labels do not show whether a mechanism is active or treatment-relevant in an individual patient. We conducted a structured critical narrative review informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles. MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and CENTRAL were searched for English-language literature published from 1 January 2015 to 7 August 2026; seminal earlier studies were identified by citation tracking. Human genetic, pathological, longitudinal biomarker, multi-omic, imaging, neurophysiological, and interventional evidence was prioritized. Evidence was appraised by human proximity, temporality, replication, mechanistic specificity, and treatment relevance. Evidence supports interacting RNA/proteostasis, nucleocytoplasmic-transport, glial-inflammatory, and energetic-metabolic processes, but current evidence does not yet support the use of any candidate state for individual treatment assignment. The most mature temporal example is loss of TDP-43 splicing repression before neurofilament elevation in genetically at-risk individuals. Nucleocytoplasmic-transport evidence is strongest in C9orf72 disease; inflammatory and metabolic signals are confounded by disease burden and systemic illness; and the gut-brain axis remains a context-dependent amplifier. We propose prespecified transition rules, evidence grades, and biomarker-by-treatment interaction tests. A state-transition model becomes clinically useful when longitudinal measurements add value beyond clinical predictors and injury markers and prospectively identify differential treatment benefit.

articles.title: Clinically unresponsive patients with acute brain injury activate a brain-computer interface.
articles.abstract: Brain activation to verbal commands can be detected by EEG in clinically unresponsive patients. These patients with cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) are unable to communicate with the environment despite preserved consciousness. Advanced brain-computer interfaces (BCI) are promising to support motor function in patients with motor neuron disease or spinal cord injury. Our primary objective was to determine if clinically unresponsive patients can control a self-paced, one-way BCI early after acute brain injury. Secondarily, we assessed the association of BCI control with short- and long-term outcomes. We conducted a prospective single-centre cohort study in 41 clinically unresponsive, critically ill and acutely brain injured patients, as well as in a convenience sample of 8 healthy volunteers and 22 conscious critically ill patients. The self-paced BCI analysed EEG in real time and modulated frequency and pitch of a tone that patients controlled by attempting a motor task: patients were provided with instructions 'to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand' alternating with 'to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand'. CMD was detected by applying machine learning to EEG recorded while patients listened to motor commands. Clinical outcomes were recovery of consciousness by hospital discharge, assessed with the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised, and recovery of functional independence at 12 months, defined as a Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score of 4 or higher (denoting the ability to function independently for 8 h or more). Additionally, we invited conscious patients as well as family members of conscious and clinically unresponsive patients to complete a survey on perceived utility and challenges associated with the BCI. In this study, 13 clinically unresponsive patients (32%) achieved BCI control and 8 of 41 (20%) were CMD-positive. All healthy volunteers and nine conscious patients (41%) were able to control the BCI. Median signal delay for BCI control was 49.8 [interquartile range (IQR) 39.9-75.6] seconds for clinically unresponsive patients, 17.1 (IQR 7.8-19.9) for conscious patients and 15.5 (IQR 12.9-21.2) for healthy volunteers. In the group of 41 clinically unresponsive patients, 4 of 13 patients with (31%) and 1 of 28 without BCI control (4%) recovered clinical consciousness at hospital discharge [odds ratio (OR) 21.2; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.3-930.7]. At 12 months, 6 of 13 patients with (46%) and 2 of 28 without BCI control (7%) recovered functional independence (OR 9.9; 95% CI 1.8-81.6). None of the patients that were unable to control the BCI and were CMD-negative recovered. Patients with BCI control had shorter times to recovery of functional independence by 12 months than those who did not (hazards ratio 6.0; 95% CI 1.2-30.6). All respondents of the BCI survey (n = 37) expressed strong support for the potential future use of BCI devices. These results suggest that BCI control is a strong predictor of outcomes following acute brain injury and provide initial evidence that a bedside, EEG-based BCI system might permit bidirectional communication in critically ill unresponsive patients.

articles.title: Tau isoform mapping across tissues and biofluids reveals a signature distinguishing Alzheimer's disease from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Blood phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) accurately detects Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology but is also elevated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), likely reflecting peripheral (big) tau released from muscle. Assays selectively measuring brain-derived (BD-) tau and BD-p-tau217 are therefore needed. We analysed serum BD-tau and p-tau217 in ALS (n = 139), AD (n = 101) and controls (n = 75) using direct immunoassays and after BD-Tau immunoprecipitation (BD-Tau-IP), and tau species in brain (n = 16), spinal cord (n = 11) and muscle (n = 10) by targeted mass spectrometry. With the direct immunoassays, BD-tau and p-tau217 were increased in AD and ALS versus controls. After BD-Tau-IP, BD-tau and BD-p-tau217 were elevated in AD only, improving diagnostic accuracy. Mass spectrometry revealed a central-to-peripheral shift from BD-tau to big tau predominance, with exclusively big p-tau217 detected in muscle. Selective detection of BD-tau species improves the specificity of blood AD biomarkers by reducing peripheral tau confounding.

articles.title: Beyond Monogenic Inheritance: Emerging Genetic Architecture of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by marked genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. Although pathogenic variants in major ALS genes, including C9ORF72 , SOD1 , TARDBP , and FUS , have provided fundamental insights into disease pathogenesis, many familial and most sporadic cases remain without a molecular diagnosis, suggesting a genetic architecture extending beyond coding variants and monogenic inheritance. Advances in genomic technologies have revealed contributions from deep-intronic and regulatory variants, structural rearrangements, repeat expansions, and other forms of genomic variation incompletely captured by standard diagnostic approaches. Evidence also indicates that combinations of rare variants with moderate or incomplete penetrance may contribute to disease susceptibility and clinical variability, supporting a multilayer model of ALS genetics. Population-specific variation and convergence of genetically diverse defects on common molecular pathways further complicate variant interpretation and disease classification. This review examines emerging components of ALS genetic architecture, including non-coding variation, structural variants, repeat expansions, oligogenic burden, ancestry-related gaps, and convergent neurodegenerative pathways. Integrating these genomic layers with functional and transcriptomic evidence may improve variant interpretation, diagnostic yield, patient stratification, and the development of mechanism-based precision therapies.

articles.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis.
articles.abstract: Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1-3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans. Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2-BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington's disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

articles.title: Cytoplasmic TDP-43 Accumulation in Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay.
articles.abstract: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) is a rare, early-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and peripheral neuropathy. It is caused by biallelic mutations in the SACS gene, which encodes sacsin, a large protein involved in cytoskeletal organization and mitochondrial homeostasis, and protein quality control. Despite advances in understanding sacsin biology, the molecular mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration in ARSACS remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the first neuropathological evidence of pathological TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) accumulation in ARSACS. Available postmortem brain tissue from a genetically confirmed ARSACS patient homozygous for the Quebec founder mutation ( SACS c.8844delT) was analyzed by immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence and biochemical fractionation. Neurons in the prefrontal cortex, motor cortex and cerebellum exhibited cytoplasmic phosphorylated dot-like TDP-43 (pTDP-43) aggregates with reduced nuclear localization. Biochemical fractionation further identified detergent-insoluble TDP-43 species in ARSACS tissue. Additional pathological features included increased neurofilament accumulation, vacuole-like neuronal changes, Purkinje cell loss and p62-positive cytoplasmic inclusions. Similar dot-like cytoplasmic pTDP-43 aggregates were observed in a second ARSACS case. These findings identify pTDP-43 as a previously unrecognized pathological feature of ARSACS. While the patient exhibited no clinical or histopathological signs of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the presence of atypical pTDP-43 aggregates observed in ARSACS may represent a rare, secondary, early-stage or potentially underrecognized manifestation of TDP-43 pathology rather than a defining hallmark of the disease. Further studies in additional patients and experimental ARSACS models will be required to determine the prevalence and mechanistic basis of TDP-43 abnormalities in this disorder.
articles.journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques

articles.title: End-of-life care of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and home mechanical ventilation: the national population-based DISCOVERY study.
articles.abstract: Background: Home mechanical ventilation (HMV), including noninvasive ventilation (NIV) and invasive ventilation (IV), is increasingly used in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (pwALS), but its impact on end-of-life care remains unclear. Objective: To examine whether ventilation pathway (NIV or IV) influences symptom prevalence and relief during the final week of life in pwALS. Secondary objectives were to assess end-of-life discussions, place and cause of death, and anticipated death. Methods: This national, population-based retrospective cohort study included pwALS using HMV in the Swedish National Quality Registry for Respiratory Failure (Swedevox), cross-linked with the Swedish Register of Palliative Care, which contains staff-reported end-of-life data, and other national registries. Results: Among 652 pwALS, 609 received NIV (mean age 66 years, 42% female) and 43 IV (mean age 60 years, 42% female). Anxiety and breathlessness were more common in the NIV group (76% vs 48% and 72% vs 31%, both p < 0.001), while prevalence and relief of other symptoms were similar between groups. Most patients had end-of-life discussions (NIV 87%, IV 92%). NIV patients more often died in specialized palliative wards (22% vs 7%, p = 0.023). Most deaths were due to ALS (96%) and were anticipated (NIV 94%, IV 88%). Conclusions: In pwALS with HVM, NIV was associated with higher rates of anxiety and breathlessness in the final week of life, but the ventilation pathway did not influence overall symptom relief. End-of-life communications and cause of death were similar; place of death differed by ventilation pathway; however, most deaths were anticipated.

articles.title: Molecular signatures of selective motor neuron vulnerability in old age.
articles.abstract: Motor neuron (MN) death and impairment of fast-fatigable motor units is widely recognized in elderly humans and rats. However, the molecular signatures identifying vulnerable MNs remains underexplored. In murine models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9) and chondrolectin (Chodl) decline with disease progression and have been considered molecular markers of fast-fatigable MNs. However, their expression in brainstem and lumbar MNs, in accordance with the 'size principle' (in which motor units are recruited in a size-dependent manner, with MNs of lower capacitance activated before those of greater capacitance) and their expression throughout the lifespan remain unclear. Here, we evaluated MMP-9 and Chodl in lumbar and hypoglossal MNs in young (6 months) and old (24 months) Fischer 344 (F344) rats. Longitudinal lumbar spinal cord transverse brainstem sections (the orientations providing maximal MN somal sizes for each pool) were immunolabelled for choline acetyltransferase, MMP-9 and Chodl. Expression was quantified using confocal microscopy in young and old rats (n = 5 females, n = 5 males per age). Overall, MMP-9 demonstrated a positive association with lumbar MN somal surface area in young rats. Paired within-animal analysis showed that in larger MNs, MMP-9 positivity was ∼70% greater than smaller MNs. The size-dependence of MMP-9 expression was absent in old lumbar MNs, suggesting either selective loss or downregulation of MMP-9 MN expression in ageing. No size-dependent change in Chodl was observed in lumbar or hypoglossal MNs, nor was MMP-9 associated with MN size in hypoglossal MNs. Collectively, these findings identify MMP-9 as a marker enriched within large lumbar MNs in young rats and suggest that age-related alterations in MMP-9 expression may reflect the selective vulnerability of the lumbar MNs.

articles.title: Neurotransmitter-defined cerebral vulnerability patterns in frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD).
articles.abstract: Frontotemporal dementia syndromes encompass a genetically, clinically and radiologically heterogeneous set of conditions with distinctive clinical and imaging characteristics. The main FTD phenotypes exhibit strikingly different disease burden patterns with a predilection to specific brain regions and relative sparing of others. The apparent selectivity of cerebral involvement in FTD has not been fully elucidated. A prospective neuroimaging study has been undertaken with a uniform imaging protocol to characterise atrophy patterns in ALS-FTD, behavioural variant FTD, nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia, and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia and evaluate associations with physiological neurotransmitter receptor expression maps. Anatomical correlations between focal volume loss and a large panel of neurotransmitters were systematically evaluated and associations ranked. Associations were noted with GABAergic, opioid, cannabinoid, microglial and acetylcholine systems in ALSFTD-C9NEG. Correlations were observed with opioid, glutaminergic, and synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A receptor populations in ALSFTD-C9POS. Atrophy in bvFTD showed predilection to serotonergic, glutaminergic, opioid, GABAergic and cannabinoid circuits. Volume loss in nfvPPA colocalised with GABAergic, opioid, microglial, serotonergic, cannabinoid, acetylcholine, glutaminergic and dopaminergic networks. A multitude of neurotransmitter populations are implicated in svPPA including opioid, serotonergic, GABAergic, dopaminergic, and microglial systems. The distinctive neuroimaging signatures of FTD phenotypes exhibit spatial associations with physiological neurotransmitter receptor density maps. The propensity of atrophy to specific brain regions in FTD subtypes may be defined by neurotransmitter populations. Our findings indirectly support the notion of neurotransmitter-system defined connectivity-based disease propagation in FTD.

articles.title: Serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 levels in adolescents and adults with 5q spinal muscular atrophy.
articles.abstract: Reliable blood biomarkers for longitudinal monitoring in adolescent and adult 5q spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) are lacking. Phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species are elevated in serum in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), where they may reflect peripheral nerve and muscle pathology. We aimed to investigate serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 as longitudinal biomarkers in adolescent and adult SMA and assessed associations with clinical parameters. In this retrospective multi-centre study, we assessed serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 levels in adults with 5q SMA under treatment with nusinersen or risdiplam, comparing levels with Alzheimer's disease (AD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and non-neurodegenerative disease controls. Associations with motor function, respiratory capacity, creatine kinase (CK), and neurofilament light chain (NfL) were assessed using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and sex. Serum p-tau181 was higher in SMA than in disease controls (β = -0.48, 95%-CI -0.81 to -0.15), but lower than in ALS (β = 0.99, 95%-CI 0.58 to 1.39) and AD (β = 0.56, 95%-CI 0.11 to 1.00). P-tau181 declined from baseline to FUP2 (Δ median -1.80 pg/mL, IQR -5.90 to 2.10); p-tau217 showed no longitudinal change. P-tau181 and p-tau217 were positively associated with motor function, functional status, respiratory capacity, and CK, with no association with NfL. In exploratory analyses, higher baseline p-tau181 was associated with greater HFMSE decline (β = 1.79, 95%-CI 0.59 to 2.99). Serum p-tau181 and p-tau217 appear to reflect ongoing muscle turnover in adult SMA, declining as muscle mass decreases. Higher baseline p-tau181 was associated with subsequent functional deterioration, suggesting potential utility as a biomarker of active denervation and disease monitoring.

articles.title: The clinical spectrum of suicide-related outcomes in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: To synthesize clinically distinct suicide-related outcomes in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and comparative suicide risk without pooling non-equivalent constructs. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, PsycINFO, the Virtual Health Library, and SciELO through March 17, 2026, and updated all searches for March 18 through October 9, 2026. We included observational reports of predefined suicide-related outcomes. Outcomes with at least 3 independent studies were pooled using random-effects generalized linear mixed models for proportions and a Hartung-Knapp model for comparative estimates. We used Joanna Briggs Institute tools and adapted GRADE. Twenty-eight reports representing 26 independent cohorts were included; 21 cohorts contributed quantitative data. Active suicidal ideation was 43% (23/53; 95% CI, 30%-58%) in an end-stage cohort and 14% (10/71; 95% CI, 7%-24%) in a general clinic cohort; these estimates were not pooled. Hypothetical consideration of assisted dying was 50% (95% CI, 41%-59%; I 2 = 49%; 95% prediction interval, 21%-79%; 4 studies). Crude suicide mortality rates were 0.16 and 0.36 per 100 person-years in 2 cohorts. Three registry or administrative cohorts yielded a relative suicide-risk estimate of 4.6 (95% CI, 2.5-8.5; 95% prediction interval, 0.4-53.6). Certainty was low or very low. Suicide-related experiences in ALS are clinically distinct. Clinicians should clarify meaning, assess intent and immediacy, evaluate decision-making capacity and treatable psychiatric symptoms, and address palliative and psychosocial needs. A death wish or assisted-dying preference should not be assumed to indicate active suicidal intent.

articles.title: Towards semantic brain-computer interfacing: The graded inventory of semantic triggers (GIST) paradigm.
articles.abstract: Semantic Brain-Computer Interfaces (sBCIs) aim to decode conceptual information directly from neural activity, enabling more efficient and natural communication for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, existing approaches are often confounded by stimulus-driven perceptual processes and lack a reliable means of tagging the moment of concept formation. We introduce the Graded Inventory of Semantic Triggers (GIST), a novel electroencephalography (EEG) paradigm designed to elicit semantic retrieval from graded verbal clues with precise temporal alignment.Approach: EEG data were recorded from 14 participants performing the GIST task across three semantic categories (food, musical instruments, and body parts). Target neural activity was aligned to each participant's self-reported moment of semantic retrieval (spacebar press), enabling response-locked analysis. Here, we propose a staged framework where the first comprises a Conformer-based encoder trained on pooled data using a hybrid contrastive objective that combines instance-level consistency and cross-participant class alignment with domain-adversarial learning to reduce participant-specific information. In the second stage, the frozen encoder is transferred to a held-out participant whose data played no part in Stage 1, and a support vector machine is calibrated on that participant's own labelled items under a nested leave-one-item-out protocol.Results: Above-chance semantic decoding was achieved in all three pairwise tasks. Mean accuracies were 73.4% (Body vs. Food), 70.7% (Body vs. Music), and 68.2% (Food vs. Music). Participant-level permutation tests were significant in 9/11 participants for Body vs. Food and 8/11 for each of the other tasks (p < 0.05). The pre-response interval at [-1.5s, -0.5s] was the most discriminative.Significance: The GIST paradigm enables controlled elicitation and temporal alignment of semantic processing while reducing perceptual confounds. Combined with cross-participant representation pretraining and participant-specific calibration, the results demonstrate above-chance decoding of semantic categories from EEG in individuals excluded from representation learning, supporting the feasibility of sBCIs.

articles.title: Understanding Holistic Patient-Relevant Measurement in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Mixed-Methods Content Validity and Exploratory Rasch Analysis of Selected Clinical Outcome Assessments.
articles.abstract: Living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) has a profound impact on function and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). This mixed-methods study aimed to cognitively debrief selected ALS outcome measures to investigate their relevance and conduct exploratory Rasch Measurement Theory (RMT) analyses to assess targeting. Semi-structured interviews were conducted (January-September 2024) with people living with ALS (PLwALS) and clinicians to cognitively debrief selected patient- and clinician-reported outcome (PRO and ClinRO) measures. The PRO measures debriefed with PLwALS were Rasch Overall ALS Disability Scale (ROADS), 5-item ALS Assessment Questionnaire (ALSAQ-5), and Neurological Fatigue Index for Motor Neurone Disease (NFI-MND). ROADS and ClinRO ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) were debriefed with clinicians. Interview transcripts were qualitatively analyzed; structured codes were used to compile data on item relevance and comprehensiveness. Exploratory RMT analysis was conducted using quantitative data from PLwALS responses to evaluate selected PRO psychometric properties. Qualitative analysis of interviews with 31 PLwALS found that PROs were meaningful and relevant, and identified the relevance of individual items. Clinicians (n = 10) endorsed ALSFRS-R as a relevant and meaningful measure, and supported ROADS' conceptual coverage and response category. RMT analysis indicated evidence of good targeting, reliability, and item fit for the PROs, with some exceptions for ALSAQ-5. This study supports the use of ALSFRS-R, ROADS, ALSAQ-5, and NFI-MND to measure meaningful aspects of ALS, with support for ALSAQ-5 qualified by its limited measurement precision. Scores from these measures can provide important insights into the lived experience of PLwALS, characterizing disease progression and HRQoL.

articles.title: "It's like saving for a rainy day": perceptions of voice banking for people living with Motor Neurone Disease.
articles.abstract: This exploratory qualitative study examined how people living with Motor Neurone Disease (PlwMND) and their partners perceived voice banking and related voice preservation counseling within a specialist Australian service. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in 2022 with five PlwMND and two partners. Participants represented varying levels of engagement with voice banking, including individuals who had completed voice banking and those who had not commenced and therefore discussed voice banking conceptually. Participants described voice banking as a means of preserving identity and social connection, while also identifying uncertainty about timing, emotional readiness, and the practical demands of early action. Variable clinician knowledge, service navigation challenges, and confusion between voice preservation methods highlight the importance of informational counseling experiences. Findings are interpreted as reflections of participant perceptions at a specific point in time and within a single service context, rather than evaluations of current technological capability. The study highlights the importance of proactive, accurate, and staged informational counseling that reflects evolving voice preservation technologies and local service pathways.

articles.title: ABCD-Trial: study protocol for a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients with Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis for the evaluation of efficacy and safety of B-Cell Depletion with rituximab (ABCD).
articles.abstract: The exact disease-causing mechanisms in ALS remain incompletely understood. A possible cause is inflammation of neurons. Compared to other neurodegenerative diseases, neuroinflammation is pronounced in ALS, presumably leading to disease progression and neuronal death. Patients with ALS can have neuronal autoantibodies and most notably antibody-producing cells in the cerebrospinal fluid. The CD20-binding therapeutic antibody rituximab targets these antibody-producing B-cells. Rituximab is a medication commonly used in neurology. Single patients with ALS have already been treated with rituximab, which was well tolerated. We therefore want to evaluate safety and efficacy of a treatment with rituximab in ALS patients in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
